slides.headline: BRAND STRATEGIST
slides.lead: I'm Florian Philippe. I help people and companies figure out what they really do, and say it clearly.
slides.notes: Section 1, self-introduction (PDF 1a, 1b). Name, title, one plain sentence on what you do. Company profile: your own brand strategy practice, working with founders and companies internationally, based in California. About a minute.

slides.headline: WHERE ARE YOU RIGHT NOW?
slides.lead: Both answers are completely fine. Most useful careers get built by people who started in the second group.
interaction: How many of you already know what career you want?
How many of you are still figuring it out?
slides.notes: Participation (PDF: encourage curiosity, questions, participation). Real show of hands. If recording, frame on yourself and the slides only, never students (T-147).

image.alt: A tidy still life of well-made objects and a notebook on concrete.

slides.headline: HOW I PREPARED
slides.lead: I studied business and entrepreneurship in Le Mans, France, then took internships in the UK and in China. I found this work by trying things.

columns.label: What I studied
items: Science and math track, French baccalaureate

slides.notes: Section 2 (PDF 2a, 2b, 2c). How I discovered it: curiosity and internships, not a plan. How I prepared: business school plus internships abroad. Keep it factual.

slides.headline: THE JOBS I HAVE HAD
slides.lead: None of these were on a list when I started. Looking back, they connect.

roles.role: Digital marketing for a French hat maker
Brand manager at a solar company

slides.projectsLabel: Things I started on the side
slides.notes: Section 3, career journey (PDF 3). Left = the jobs, including the six-month Vietnam marketing manager role I hated but learned from. Right = side projects, each $0 (talk through the point out loud, the slide just shows the zeros): backing tracks for musicians (2014); NFC business cards (2018, people asked me to make them, I didn't believe in it, startups raised millions later); finding my own clients (2025, the consulting was fine, the marketing of it flopped, zero leads). The $0 is the motivational point: trying and failing is normal and fine.

image.alt: Florian Philippe presenting at the front of a room, beside a projected slide.

slides.headline: WHAT I ACTUALLY DO
slides.lead: A brand strategist helps people and companies say what they do clearly. A normal day:
examples: Talk to a founder about what they actually do.
Find the one true sentence that explains them.
Cut everything that is not that.
slides.point: Most businesses do not have a design problem first. They have a clarity problem.
slides.notes: Day-to-day responsibilities (PDF 3a). Concrete: this answers what you do all day.

slides.headline: I SIT ON THE CREATIVE SIDE
slides.lead: Brand strategy is a wide job, done many different ways. Mine leans creative, closer to a designer than a marketer.
examples: Most marketing work is ads, sales, or operations.
I work on identity, message, and how a brand looks and sounds.
slides.notes: Company info, what the work is actually like (PDF). Position on the creative/design side so the marketing and sales students do not get the wrong impression. Brand strategy is done many ways; yours is one specific, creative version. Takeaway: find your own version, do not copy mine.

slides.headline: WHERE A BRAND STRATEGIST SITS
slides.lead: Modern marketing is really four kinds of people in one room. My job is to move between them and keep the work pointing the same way.
slides.spanDesc: I move across all four and keep them pointing the same way.
slides.notes: The marketing world as Florian sees it: creative, strategy, data, AI people. He is the connector who moves between them. Use to show students the field is bigger and more visual than they think, and there is a place in it for many kinds of person.

slides.eyebrow: STARTING OUT, AND WHAT WAS HARD
slides.headline: SOME OF IT WAS HARD
slides.lead: The early years were not glamorous.
examples: Moving to new countries where I knew no one.
Freelancing in Vietnam with very little money.
Learning by getting things wrong with real clients first.
slides.point: None of it felt like a plan at the time.
slides.notes: What it was like starting and professional challenges (PDF 3b, 3c). Be honest, not a lecture.

slides.headline: SKILLS THAT HELP IN ALMOST ANY CAREER
skills: Using tools without becoming the tool
slides.notes: Skills in Florian's voice (PDF 2c). MAKING FRIENDS: the network you build from high school on, friends in many countries, referrals run both ways; don't be afraid to mix the professional and the personal, the job lasts a few years but the friendship can last forever. ASKING STUPID QUESTIONS: the ones everyone is too scared to ask, usually half the room did not know either, and it is devil's advocate. DOING WHAT NOBODY ELSE DOES: 'It is not that hard to be number one. You just have to find something nobody else does.' (Generalist by nature, envies deep specialists, the resolution is finding your own lane.) Prompt: one skill you could practice this summer that helps in more than one career?

image.alt: A precisely machined metal piece on concrete with a purple sheen.

slides.headline: GOOD WORK IS NOT ENOUGH
slides.lead: For years I believed good work would speak for itself. It does not. The most talented people I know stay best-kept secrets, waiting to be discovered.
slides.point: What makes you special is showing up and showing the work. Even more now that AI can fake the result in seconds.
slides.notes: The biggest lesson, deliver it big. Best-kept-secrets: most talented people are waiting to be discovered, like actors waiting for a break. The crush line lands with teens (a client, a promotion, your crush: standing there doing good work and looking nice is not enough, people expect more). The bag example for perception. We all want to feel special; the thing that makes us special is what we do constantly, and that we show up and show it. Tie to AI: it can fake the finished product in seconds, so the showing-up matters more, not less.

slides.headline: FIND A CAUSE, NOT (JUST) A PURPOSE
slides.lead: A purpose is heavy and lonely. A cause is something you can join. Three ways in:
interaction: What impact do you want to make in your community?
slides.notes: Cause and reflection combined. Reframe out loud: everyone is told to find a unique purpose, and that pressure freezes them, because it is hard to be that unique. A cause is lighter, you find and join it. Florian's own: help every business feel like no other, glad when anyone gets there. Then the three PDF questions (4b) as the way in, read slowly, invite a couple to share.

slides.headline: WHICH ONE ARE YOU?
slides.lead: Put a team in a room and each person quietly protects something different:
slides.point: Notice which one is you. It is the first clue to what you are good at.
slides.notes: Specialist vs generalist did not land; this is the better version. In any team people protect different things, often regardless of title: being heard and included, getting it done, keeping order, keeping it safe, making it beautiful (that is me). Have them notice their own default, what they reach for at play, the games they like, when they hit flow. That orientation is the first signal of where they fit. Speak it; the slide just lists the types.
